First, CFSN 2 extracts momentum-updated feature queues for both global and local representations, enabling temporally coherent and stable similarity estimation. Second, it models dual-granularity similarity distributions via Gaussian Mixture Models and detects potential FNs through probabilistic cross-granularity consensus. Finally, the detected FNs are dynamically reweighted based on their FN confidence, softly suppressing their gradients while preserving informative negatives for a balanced optimization process. Extensive experiments across three datasets show that CFSN 2 achieves strong overall retrieval performance, with R@1 scores of 19.12, 28.96, and 22.86 in image-to-text retrieval, and 15.02, 25.22, and 18.00 in text-to-image retrieval, respectively, compared with 26 baselines.

title: SAMWater: a prompt-guided multimodal framework for transferable water mapping with the segment anything model
abstract: Accurate and transferable surface water mapping is critical for water resource assessment, flood monitoring, and aquatic ecosystem management, but remains difficult because SAR speckle, optical contamination, heterogeneous backgrounds, and scarce high-quality pixel-level annotations limit robust large-scale mapping. We propose SAMWater, a prompt-guided multimodal framework that integrates Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical imagery, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3). Instead of using SAR and optical data as independent classifiers, SAMWater transforms their complementary information into structured prompts for coarse-to-refined water segmentation. A physically interpretable multisensor coarse water prior is first generated from Sentinel observations using an automatic threshold-based strategy. This prior is then refined through prompt-based boundary refinement, a multi-prompt excavation strategy that derives point, box, and Gaussian-style mask prompts, and Water-IoU fine-tuning for water-specific candidate ranking. Using globally distributed samples and manually interpreted PlanetScope reference labels, SAMWater achieved average Kappa coefficients of 90.71%, 85.63%, and 89.05% in evaluations stratified by water body type, land cover background, and climatic zone, respectively. It generally outperformed traditional thresholding and clustering methods, public deep learning models, and existing global water or land cover products, particularly in structurally complex river, reservoir, urban, agricultural, and mountainous scenes. Ablation experiments confirmed that multimodal prior fusion, structured prompt construction, and water-specific ranking jointly drive the performance gains. Moreover, SAMWater-generated refined labels improved the training of U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and SegFormer, indicating their utility for weakly supervised segmentation. SAMWater therefore demonstrates that integrating physically interpretable remote sensing priors with promptable foundation models provides a practical pathway for transferable surface water mapping, large-scale multisensor weak-label generation, and more consistent monitoring of surface water extent.

Beyond the Snowflakes: Disentangling Weather Effects from Confounding Meta-Factors in LiDAR Object Detection
abstract: Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) is critical for autonomous perception, yet its performance is known to degrade in adverse weather. While existing literature models snow as atmospheric noise that degrades performance, our granular evaluation on the WADS-3D and CADC datasets reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: detection accuracy consistently improves as snow intensity increases. Through ablation study and meta-information analysis, we reconcile this by confirming that while falling snow acts as noise, its negative impact is outweighed by a dominant, concurrent factor: significantly increased object point count. We hypothesize that this object point count boost acts as a geometric enhancement, driven by snow accumulation increasing vehicle surface area and a shift from specular to diffuse reflectance. Our findings demonstrate that evaluating perception systems using broad weather-severity bins without accounting for correlated object-level data can lead to misleading conclusions about detector robustness. We conclude that accurate evaluation requires decoupling atmospheric noise from surface accumulation effects and outline future research to validate these physical models. The WADS-3D dataset is available at: https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/wads-3d/.

title: Revisiting the Task of Building Damage Assessment by Satellite Imaging
abstract: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, tropical storms, and floods cause extensive damage to buildings, and rapid, reliable damage maps are essential to guide emergency response. Automating this task, referred to as building damage assessment (BDA), from satellite imagery, has become an active research topic at the intersection of remote sensing, computer vision, and machine learning, particularly since supervised deep learning methods were shown to outperform earlier handcrafted approaches. Yet, despite a decade of intense activity and the release of several large-scale datasets, the field lacks a shared foundation. This chapter revisits the task of BDA from first principles, organized around three pillars: data, evaluation, and methods. We first clarify the candidate task for- mulations and argue for a sensor-agnostic, instance-based definition that tolerates missing pre-event imagery. We then review existing datasets along the axes of sensing modality, temporal configuration, and geographic coverage. On the evaluation side, we show that prevailing practices, largely based on a single aggregate score, are theoretically fragile, and we lay the foundations of a more informative, ranking-based, multi-score protocol. We further review methods ranging from task-specific deep networks to recent Earth observation foundation models, noticing that generalization to unseen events and regions remains an open difficulty. Finally, we discuss how these elements can inform the organization of a BDA challenge, including cross-validation, challenge, and private data-sharing setups designed to build trust between developers and users.

title: Event-based Action Recognition by Pre-Training on Multi-Frame Representations
abstract: Action recognition is a crucial task in domains like robotics, patient monitoring, or surveillance. Recently, event-based action recognition has attracted much attention due to the event camera's ability to capture fast motions and its improved privacy over conventional vision cameras. While frame-based event representations work well for short event sequences, their discriminative ability declines sharply with longer and more complex event sequences. In this work, we introduce a multi-frame representation that greatly improves recognition performance over its single-frame counterpart. We adopt a masked auto-encoding framework to pre-train a Vision Transformer using a sparsity-aware masking algorithm and token selection mechanism to improve downstream performance and control computational complexity. We also introduce multiple mask tokens for the decoder with a position-aware attention mechanism, leading to further improved performance. Our proposed method shows impressive performance for challenging long-duration and complex event sequences, yielding state-of-the-art performance on THU-EACT-50 CHL and DailyDVS-200.

title: DIA: A Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Interest-Aware ABR Scheme for Cloud Gaming
abstract: The continuous evolution of cloud gaming has enabled users to play high-quality cloud games on thin clients, such as smartphones and tablets. However, how to effectively transmit the gameplay frames with high resolution and low latency, especially over wireless networks, remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based Interest-Aware Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) scheme, called DIA, that guarantees the quality of perceptually key objects in each frame, while dynamically allocating lower resolutions for non-key objects to conserve bandwidth under constrained network conditions. By leveraging an off-the-shelf semantic segmentation model, the proposed DIA scheme can adjust the bitrate at the object-level. We also design a transformer-based feature extractor and an interest-aware reward function to enable the proposed DIA scheme to identify key objects and dynamically adjust their bitrates. This adaptation is guided by users' in-game movement speed, object features, and prevailing network conditions and operates without requiring additional hardware, such as gaze trackers. Extensive experiments show that the proposed DIA scheme outperforms existing ABR schemes in dynamic wireless network environments. Notably, DIA achieves at least a 20% higher normalized average Quality of Experience (QoE) than the State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) ABR algorithms in 5G scenarios.

title: Improving Semantic Coverage in AI Test & Evaluation through Generative Augmentation
abstract: In test and evaluation (T&E) of AI models, evaluators typically have access only to a held-out test dataset and no knowledge of the training data or its semantic composition. If critical input conditions---such as time-of-day, weather, or scene location---are underrepresented in this test dataset, T&E results can be misleadingly due to this semantic coverage gap. We propose a three-stage generative AI pipeline to detect and fill such semantic gaps without requiring ground-truth labels of these semantics. First, vision-language models (VLMs) perform zero-shot binary labeling of semantic factors, and an embedding-space clustering step identifies which semantics most affect downstream model behavior. Second, diffusion-based image-to-image models transform existing covered images into the underrepresented semantic domain, preserving scene content while augmenting high-level appearance. Third, statistical analysis of the augmented image embeddings verifies that the synthetic imagery improves dataset coverage before it is incorporated. Crucially, the synthetic data is used only to enrich the test set and no model retraining is performed for T&E. We validate the full pipeline on both image classification and object detection under day/night semantic gaps, showing that the augmented test datasets better distinguish models with and without exposure to the missing semantic, thereby yielding T&E conclusions that more closely match those of an ideal, fully covered dataset. Code available at https://github.com/Hashe037/DEDUCE

title: Benchmarking Answer-Grounding Consistency in Remote Sensing Visual Question Answering
abstract: In grounded remote sensing visual question answering, a model produces a textual answer and identifies relevant objects in the image as grounding evidence. Existing evaluations measure answer correctness and localization quality, but do not directly assess answer-grounding consistency. We propose the Answer-Evidence Support Protocol (AESP) to assess this consistency through evidence support: whether the grounding evidence supports the model's own answer. AESP applies task-specific rules to existence, counting, and comparison questions. We further construct the Grounded Remote Sensing Visual Question Answering (G-RSVQA) benchmark, containing 15,027 samples with questions, reference answers, and all related object-level annotations. Experiments on seven grounded vision--language models reveal failures of evidence support across all three question types. Up to 50.82% of correct answers in the evidence evaluation subset are not supported by the provided grounding evidence.

title: Warning of infrastructure deformation anomaly through probabilistic analysis of InSAR observations
abstract: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) offers a low-cost, wide-area solution for near continuous infrastructure monitoring. However, translating InSAR observations into automated anomaly warnings remains challenging because displacements are relative, affected by uncertainty, and acquired along line of sight (LOS). We introduced a probabilistic warning framework that accounts for these factors. LOS displacements were modelled through a Gaussian distribution. A limit state function was defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance was evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings were identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework was validated using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.

title: MOSAIC: Multi-Scale Object-Centric Slot Adaptation with Image-Guided Prototype Conditioning for Remote Sensing Image Super-Resolution
abstract: Pretrained diffusion Transformers provide powerful generative priors for image restoration, yet adapting them to structure-sensitive tasks remains challenging. Existing methods mainly rely on dense low-resolution features as conditions, which often entangle salient objects with dominant backgrounds and provide limited abstraction for recurring structures across scales and samples. We propose MOSAIC, an object-centric representation learning framework that learns compact structural conditions for generative model adaptation. MOSAIC organizes degraded observations into structural slots that capture complementary object-level and layout-level evidence, integrates them across resolutions, and retrieves recurring priors from a shared prototype memory to complement incomplete image-specific information. The resulting representations are injected into selected layers of a frozen diffusion Transformer through lightweight residual modulation, preserving its pretrained generative prior. We instantiate MOSAIC for remote sensing image super-resolution, where small objects, repetitive structures, and large-scale variation provide a challenging testbed. Experiments on UCMerced, AID, and RSSCN7 show consistent PSNR improvements across $\times 2$ and $\times 4$ settings and favorable LPIPS results at $\times 4$. Qualitative results further demonstrate improved preservation of small objects, structural boundaries, and repetitive spatial patterns.

title: First Experimental Results of Space Object Detection Using the InteRFeX Array
abstract: This paper presents the first experimental validation of InteRFeX, a non-uniform receive only (passive) array located at the Nova Systems Space Precinct in Peterborough, Australia, designed for space domain awareness applications. It operates over a frequency range of 70 to 300 MHz and is capable of functioning in a range of observational modes, including as a coherent passive bistatic radar for space surveillance, which is the focus of this work. InteRFeX exploits commercial broadcast transmissions as illuminators of opportunity, combining cross-ambiguity function processing for bistatic range and range-rate retrieval with MUSIC-based direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation for angular localization. The International Space Station (ISS) serves as the experimental target, with measurements evaluated against Two-Line Element (TLE) orbit predictions. Taking advantage of the dual-polarized array, all four reference--surveillance polarization combinations are evaluated, revealing differences in detection rate and mean signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) over the observation pass, with bistatic-range RMSEs of approximately 1 km relative to the TLE-derived reference. Independently, the MUSIC-based DoA estimates exhibit a mean angular separation of approximately $0.45^\circ$ from the TLE-derived reference directions. The angular deviations are further decomposed into along-track and cross-track components, enabling a more detailed characterization of the DoA offsets relative to the TLE-derived reference trajectory. The processing framework also includes a first-order bistatic link-budget analysis to estimate the expected SNR over the observation geometry. These results demonstrate the feasibility of passive-radar space domain awareness using radio-interferometric array technology and establish the proposed signal-processing pipeline as a basis for a dedicated coherent passive-radar mode within InteRFeX.

title: Knowing Whether, Not Just Where: Anchor-Probing Distillation for Open-Set Remote Sensing Visual Grounding
abstract: Open-set visual grounding in remote sensing requires models to determine not only where a queried object is located, but also whether the image provides sufficient evidence for the query at all. Existing closed-set grounding models, however, tend to return plausible boxes even for absent objects, blurring localization confidence with genuine Visual Support. We introduce AnchorProbe-Distill (APD), a teacher-student framework that recasts open-set grounding as Visual Support learning. APD builds on the insight that supported queries should induce coherent spatial anchors, whereas unsupported or mismatched queries tend to produce unstable or misleading localization patterns. APD-T therefore uses the Original Query as a Reference Anchor to interpret query perturbations: Semantic-Preserving Queries retain the annotated target, Near-Category Ambiguous Queries are resolved according to whether they form a reliable alternative anchor or collapse onto the Reference Anchor, and Far-Category Counterfactual Queries provide rejection supervision. This reference-aware reasoning is distilled into APD-S, enabling unified localization and rejection from a single image--query pair. Experiments show that APD enables the resulting model to reject absent targets while also improving its localization of present targets.

title: Decoding Register Tokens Preserves Global Scene Details
abstract: Pretrained vision transformers learn structured image representations spanning spatial patch tokens and non-spatial tokens. Recent analyses suggest that non-spatial register tokens encode global scene properties such as illumination, blur, and style. Yet patch-based image decoders discard these outputs, leaving the decoder to recover image appearance from patches alone. We investigate whether retaining register features improves decoding when the complete spatial patch representation is already available. We study this question using representation autoencoders (RAEs) with frozen register-equipped encoders. Our decoder processes four register tokens together with all patch tokens through joint self-attention. Appearance probes, paired reconstruction-error analysis, and fixed-decoder register substitutions examine which global image properties are accessible from registers and how their values affect reconstructed pixels. For generation, we train a multi-head attention pooling (MHAP) predictor to recover register features from sampled patches, keeping the pretrained diffusion model and its samples unchanged. On ImageNet-1K, our ViT-B decoders achieve mean reconstruction FIDs of 0.472 with DINOv2 and 0.442 with DINOv3, reductions of 9.5% and 5.2% relative to their respective patch-only baselines. The corresponding PSNRs are 19.73 and 20.54 dB. For generation, our DINOv2 models achieve a mean FID of 1.641, 9.8% below the patch-only baseline on identical sampled patches.

title: Vision Transformers Learn Word Meaning from Images Alone
abstract: Can a vision model learn what words mean from pixels alone? We show that the two largest DINOv3 vision transformers organize words rendered in images by word meaning, despite being pretrained using self-supervision on images only, without paired captions, class labels, or other language supervision. We derive word representations from embedding differences between word images and matched controls, then test whether semantically related words are neighbors within each model's embedding space, while controlling for spelling similarity. We find that brand names in the same industry group together, as do nouns from the same semantic domain. Country-capital pairs exhibit consistent vector offsets, similarly to word embeddings trained on text. These word representations also align with the representations of the visual object categories they name. DINOv3-H and DINOv3-7B are, to our knowledge, the first self-supervised vision models to show substantial semantic structure for rendered words. Comparisons with text and speech encoders reveal shared structure among representations of the same words. Contrastive alignment with either encoder further strengthened DINOv3-H's word-level semantic structure, while leaving the other finetuned vision models largely unchanged. Image-only training can therefore teach vision models not just what words look like, but also how their meanings relate.

title: Comparison of NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) surface reflectance products with MODIS NBAR
abstract: Frequent surface reflectance measurements at fine spatial resolutions are crucial for land surface monitoring. The NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) project addresses this need by combining data from Landsat and Sentinel-2 missions to provide 30-m surface reflectance products with a global average revisit frequency of 2-3 days. This study evaluates the consistency of the HLS Version 2 (V2.0) product against the established Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Nadir Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function-Adjusted Reflectance (NBAR) dataset. We found a high degree of consistency between HLS and MODIS NBAR, with strong positive correlations across all six common spectral bands (R 2 values: 0.939–0.986). Globally, mean absolute differences (MADs) were generally low, typically under 0.03 for visible bands and below 0.05 for NIR and SWIR bands. However, we observed band-dependent discrepancies, with higher discrepancies in the blue and SWIR1 bands. Spatially, substantial differences were found in polar regions, largely due to isolated snow, ice, and water which are fractional and hard to detect within the coarser MODIS pixels but are filtered out in the HLS data. This finding suggests a potential explanation for past disagreements in vegetation trend analyses involving the use of satellite data of different spatial resolutions, as coarser-resolution datasets may mischaracterize greening trends in areas with partial snow and ice cover. These insights are vital for helping users interpret HLS data more effectively and for refining multi-sensor data fusion methods. Our research also provides a valuable baseline for ongoing quality assessment of the HLS product for applications such as vegetation monitoring, land management, and disaster response.

title: Degeneracy-resilient LiDAR-inertial SLAM for autonomous tunnel inspection robots
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Reliable localization and mapping remain challenging for autonomous tunnel inspection because satellite positioning is unavailable and repetitive geometric structures weaken LiDAR constraints. This work presents a tightly coupled LiDAR-inertial SLAM framework that combines intensity-assisted feature extraction, degeneracy handling, and factor-graph optimization with switchable constraints. Geometric and intensity cues are jointly used to strengthen scan matching, weakly constrained directions are identified to restrict unreliable LiDAR updates while retaining inertial predictions, and switchable constraints reduce the influence of erroneous loop closures during global optimization. The framework was evaluated on 20 sequences from the Kimera-Multi dataset, comprising 13 non-tunnel and 7 tunnel sequences, and in field scenes. On this common subset, the proposed method achieved an average absolute trajectory error (ATE) of 3.875 m, a mean rotation error (MRE) of 0.598°, and a mean map entropy (MME) of −6.431. Compared with GLIM, the best-performing baseline overall, these results correspond to reductions of 5.05 % in ATE and 4.78 % in MRE, together with an absolute decrease of 0.130 in MME. The average point-cloud registration time was 15.3 ms per frame, supporting real-time operation on the evaluated platform. Overall, this work provides a practical localization and mapping framework for autonomous robotic inspection in underground tunnels.

title: Nationwide deadwood mapping reveals rising mountain forests vulnerability
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Forest mortality is increasing globally under climate change, making detailed, large-scale monitoring essential for understanding ecosystem responses and guiding adaptive forest management. Here, we present a spatio-temporal assessment of standing deadwood in Switzerland from 2018 to 2023, derived from centimeter-scale high-resolution aerial imagery. We reveal a consistent upslope concentration of standing deadwood, with highest shares occurring around mid to high elevations (∼1,500 m), despite declining forest cover, and relative increases of up to 43% in overlapping survey areas following the 2018 drought. Maximum temperature anomalies and conifer dominance were the strongest predictors of standing deadwood. The consistent accumulation of standing deadwood at higher elevations suggests increasing vulnerability of mountain forests, with implications for carbon storage, biodiversity, and disturbance susceptibility under ongoing climate change. These patterns highlight the need to address rising forest mortality as a key component of climate-adaptive forest management. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the potential of high-resolution remote sensing for large-scale forest mortality monitoring. Our methods offer a reproducible and transferable framework for identifying vulnerability hotspots and supporting climate-adapted forest management.

title: Tracking vegetation disturbance, recovery, and sustainability in open-pit mining areas of Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei Region from 2000 to 2024
abstract: Evaluating the overarching efficacy of mine greening initiatives and supporting land resource management within open-pit mining areas requires accurate long-term monitoring of both vegetative degradation and its subsequent regenerative phases. Overcoming the bottlenecks of conventional methods in decoupling vegetation abrupt disturbances from gradual recovery processes, this research utilizes the Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Landsat data spanning from 2000 to 2024. The investigation explicitly targets open-pit mining areas across the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region. Through the synergistic integration of the Continuous Change Detection and Classification (CCDC) and an adaptively refined NDVImed,t segmentation baseline, we extracted the spatiotemporal dynamics of abrupt vegetation disturbance and gradual recovery events. Furthermore, to rigorously quantify the enduring stability and long-term persistence of these vegetation dynamic trajectories, the study coupled the non-parametric Sen–MK trend estimator with calculations of the Hurst exponent. The results demonstrate that the F1 score for detecting disturbance and recovery events over the past 25 years stably exceeded 0.8, exhibiting excellent temporal robustness. The derived chronological trajectories pinpoint 2013 as a significant turning point for vegetation dynamics. Before this critical juncture, the landscape suffered from intense degradation, marked by an average annual vegetative deficit of 962.19 ha. In the post-2013 era, a recovery-dominated paradigm emerged, characterized by an average yearly restoration of 831.37 ha. Crucially, the aggregate intensity of this vegetation greenness reached 1.64, substantially overshadowing the historical extraction-induced disturbance magnitude of 1.23. Concurrently, evaluations of trajectory persistence reveal that while a substantial 36.56% of the monitored landscape is undergoing sustained ecological enhancement, whereas 22.46% was characterized by persistent deterioration. Precipitation and temperature showed a limited influence on vegetation dynamics (R2 = 0.0796, p = 0.402), while enterprise consolidation and reclamation policies were the main drivers for post-2013 recovery. The acquired quantitative remote sensing evidence not only reveals the core role of macro-policy regulation in driving the reshaping of surface landscapes in mining areas but also provides solid scientific support for the future refined ecological governance of regional territorial space.

title: A review of remote sensing for agricultural drought: technologies, indices, modelling advances and future prospects
abstract: Agricultural drought is a complex hazard that jeopardises food security and progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. We systematically reviewed peer-reviewed English-language literature published between 2015 and 2025, focusing on Remote Sensing (RS)-driven agricultural drought monitoring and prediction. Eligible studies were identified from the Web of Science and Scopus databases (last searched in August 2025); review articles, duplicates, and irrelevant studies were excluded, resulting in 181 articles. This review critically examined the evolution of sensors, drought indices, modelling approaches, and emerging technologies used to assess agricultural drought across diverse agro-ecological regions. Specifically, we (1) systematically evaluated the use of optical, thermal, and microwave RS platforms, along with satellite-based, model-based, and reanalysis products for agricultural drought monitoring; (2) reviewed widely used RS-based drought indices, including single indices grouped into nine categories, as well as composite indices; (3) reviewed software or programming languages applied; (4) assessed the progression of modelling approaches from traditional statistical and time-series methods to machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) frameworks; and (5) examined validation strategies applied to agricultural drought assessment. The analysis reveals a growing research interest in this topic, with a strong geographic concentration in Asia, particularly China. Optical and thermal platforms (e.g. MODIS and Landsat) dominate the literature (~54%) due to their accessibility, followed by satellite-derived precipitation products (17%), while microwave soil-moisture missions remain underutilized (~7%). Regarding RS-based indices, most studies employed more than one index: 44% analysed multiple individual indices, 51% used composite indices (either alone or in combination with individual indices), and only 5% relied on a single index. Vegetation indices, such as NDVI, remain workhorses; however, their sensitivity to soil background effects and canopy saturation has driven increased adoption of thermal composites (e.g. VHI), as well as adaptive weighting schemes and principal component analysis-based approaches. Moreover, computational tools used in drought research can be broadly grouped into geospatial and RS platforms for large-scale data processing and analysis (e.g. QGIS, GEE), and general-purpose programming languages (e.g. R, Python) for model development and advanced analytics. Regarding the methodology, statistical and time-series approaches account for 64% of the reviewed studies, followed by ML models (20%) and DL methods (15%), while explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains nascent. Techniques, such as random forests, support vector machines, and CNN and LSTM architectures, generally outperform traditional models but require large training datasets and raise concerns related to interpretability and ethics. In terms of validation, hydro-climatic indices such as SPI and SPEI are most commonly used (32%), followed by crop yield and yield anomaly data (19%). This review further identifies key research gaps across sensors, indices, and modelling approaches and proposes a roadmap for developing equitable, interpretable, and resilient agricultural drought monitoring systems. Emerging opportunities include context-aware and interpretable AI, multi-sensor and multi-scale data fusion across optical, thermal, and microwave domains, integration of physiologically meaningful indicators such as sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), robust uncertainty quantification, and the development of hybrid and physics-informed modelling frameworks.
