However, reconstructing high-fidelity building polygon meshes from airborne LiDAR point clouds remains challenging due to the non-uniform and variable-sided nature of polygonal topology and the complexity of urban environments characterized by diverse building geometries, uneven point densities, and occlusions. In this paper, we present PC2Mesh, a learning-based method that reconstructs polygonal building meshes directly from airborne LiDAR point clouds. While existing approaches rely on primitive detection (e.g., City3D, Point2Poly) or employ separate networks for vertex and face generation (e.g., Point2building), our method employs a unified transformer-based architecture that jointly learns mesh geometry and topology within a shared representation space. By representing arbitrary-sided polygons as learned token sequences, the method enables holistic mesh generation without preprocessing or handcrafted priors. This end-to-end formulation mitigates error propagation across stages and enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness. Comprehensive experiments on open-source datasets demonstrate that our proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in geometric accuracy and visual fidelity. Our method improves Edge Precision (EP) and Edge Recall (ER) by 9.1% and 24.7%, respectively, on the Zurich dataset, and by 8.3% and 20.2% on the Tallinn dataset. It also achieves the lowest Mean Distance Error (MDE), Hausdorff Distance (HD), and Chamfer Distance (CD) on both datasets. The source code of this work is freely available at https://github.com/BestyHon/PC2Mesh .

title: Topology-preserving river vectorization via HydroSAM and differentiable graph optimization under coarse labels
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate river-network extraction supports global hydrological management and environmental monitoring. Automated extraction from remote-sensing imagery remains challenging because river morphology is highly variable, fine tributaries have weak visual signals, canopy and infrastructure can obscure channels, and dense annotations are scarce or spatially incomplete. Conventional raster predictions can also be fragmented and lack structural continuity. We present HydroSAM, a three-stage framework for raster extraction and topology-aware vectorization. A frozen SAM 2 Hiera encoder is adapted with QV-LoRA and the proposed Directional Curvilinear Prior Injection (DCPI), while a gated Digital Elevation Model (DEM) branch contributes coarse-scale topographic context. Segmentation is produced in a zero-prompt setting by the native SAM 2 mask decoder. A graph-guided differentiable vectorization stage then converts probability maps into connected parametric river networks. We also present M2Hydro, a benchmark containing 7,947 high-resolution 4096 × 4096 source image-annotation pairs across China. In single-run tests, HydroSAM-MM attains an F1 of 0.6995 and clDice of 0.7753 on M2Hydro. The evaluations indicate that HydroSAM supports parameter-efficient adaptation and is more resilient to the evaluated cross-regional domain shift than the convolutional and Transformer baselines.

title: Thinking on maps: how foundation model agents explore, remember, and reason in map environments
abstract: Map environments provide a fundamental medium for representing spatial structure and supporting navigation, planning, and geographic analysis. Understanding how foundation model (FM) agents acquire, consolidate, and utilize spatial knowledge in such environments is therefore critical for enabling reliable map-based reasoning and applications. However, most existing evaluations assess spatial ability in passive and non-interactive settings, without requiring models to actively explore environments, accumulate observations, and progressively construct spatial knowledge. Consequently, how spatial knowledge is formed during exploration and used for reasoning remains poorly understood. In this paper, we propose an interactive evaluation framework to examine how FM agents explore, remember, and reason in symbolic map environments. Agents incrementally navigate partially observable grid-based maps composed of roads, intersections, and points of interest (POIs), receiving only local observations at each step. Spatial understanding is then evaluated through a suite of tasks, including direction judgement, distance estimation, proximity judgement, POI density recognition, and path planning. By systematically varying exploration strategies, memory representations, and reasoning schemes across multiple foundation models, we identify distinct functional roles of these components. Exploration mainly affects experience acquisition but has a limited influence on final reasoning accuracy. In contrast, memory representation plays a central role in consolidating spatial experience, with structured memories—particularly sequential and graph-based forms—substantially improving performance on structure-intensive tasks such as path planning. Reasoning schemes further shape how stored spatial knowledge is utilized, with advanced prompting strategies supporting stronger multi-step inference. We also observe performance saturation across model versions and scales beyond a certain capability threshold, suggesting that further gains in map-based spatial understanding may depend more on spatially specialized representations and reasoning mechanisms than on model scaling alone. Overall, this work advances process-oriented evaluation of spatial cognition in FM agents and offers practical insights for building more reliable map-based reasoning systems.

title: Assessing heat dome effects on forest dynamics in the Pacific Northwest using Planet imagery
abstract: Abstract Increasingly frequent extreme heat events are imposing significant stress on forest ecosystems, with implications for forests and the organisms that live in them. This study evaluates the effects of the June 2021 Pacific Northwest (PNW) heatdome (a prolonged high-pressure system that generated record-breaking temperatures) on forest canopy health and its subsequent recovery within the conifer-dominated Ellsworth Creek Preserve in Washington state, USA, using high-resolution Planet Labs satellite imagery. We analyzed normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) trends from spring to fall from 2017 to 2024 to identify canopy stress and quantify changes in canopy greenness. Experimental forest restoration thinning treatments implemented to test their effectiveness in restoring old-growth forest characteristics at our sites allowed us to assess impacts of the heatdome event relative to these restoration treatments. Our results show a marked decline in summer NDVI following the 2021 heatdome, signaling substantial canopy stress. This decline, different than patterns in the other seven years, was particularly strong in dense, unmanaged (control) forest stands, which exhibited more pronounced NDVI declines than thinned (treatment) stands. These more pronounced stress signals during and after the heat event were associated with greater tree canopy height, canopy complexity, and tree density. The summer NDVI trends over the three post-heatdome years suggest a gradual recovery in tree canopy greenness, with thinned stands showing faster NDVI recovery than controls. In all, these results suggest that restoration thinning may improve canopy resilience to extreme heat. However, recovery trajectories varied widely within stand types, with persistent evidence of stress in high-density areas that suggest incomplete recovery as of 2023. Broadly, these findings show the vulnerability of dense forest canopies to extreme heat events, suggesting that forests with high canopy density may be less adaptable to recurring heat events. Nonetheless, managing forests through restoration thinning may enhance forest resilience to these climate-induced stressors – providing potential guidance for adaptive management strategies to maintain forest health in a world with more extreme climates.

title: Limited local classification performance but promising spatial transferability of AlphaEarth Foundations for crop mapping across thermal gradients
Evaluating spectral unmixing techniques using imaging spectroscopy data for retrieval of green, non-photosynthetic vegetation, and soil fractional cover
abstract: Estimates of fractional cover of green vegetation (GV), non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV), and soil provide valuable information about the Earth system. As the new generation of Earth visible-to-shortwave infrared (VSWIR) imaging spectrometers take orbit, global fractional cover data will be obtainable with new and improved spectral unmixing algorithms. Using an ASD Field Spectrometer and the spectral line point intercept (SLPIT) method, we estimate fractional cover from field measurements to compare to contemporaneous airborne (Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer; AVIRIS NG ) and spaceborne (Earth surface Mineral dust source InvesTigation; EMIT) imaging spectroscopy data. Field data were collected in multiple biomes in the US Southwest at 84 validation sites. We used EndMember Combination Monte Carlo (E(MC) 2 ) and Multiple-Endmember Spectral Mixture Analysis (MESMA) to derive fractional cover, two candidate spectral unmixing algorithms used by current (e.g., EMIT) and future imaging spectroscopy missions. Field data exhibited strong agreement between ground and spaceborne/airborne measurements. Our best spectral unmixing approach, E(MC) 2 , produced mean absolute error of ≤0.05 for NPV, GV, and soil with uncertainties ≤0.08 for all classes. We further investigated the performance of global vs. local endmember libraries and found that the global library outperformed the local endmember library. We investigated normalization techniques and their effectiveness with our ground and image fractions. Additionally, we calculated uncertainties from both ground and image fractions. Field results aligned well and within uncertainty predictions from previously reported simulation work. These findings support the use of E(MC) 2 to be used in current and future imaging spectroscopy missions.

title: Elevation-dependent regulation of alpine vegetation productivity by snow cover and grazing on the Tibetan Plateau under a warming–wetting climate
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Grassland productivity on the Tibetan Plateau (TP) is fundamental to regional carbon cycling and ecosystem functioning and is strongly regulated by snow dynamics and grazing under a changing climate. However, the mechanisms by which alpine grassland productivity responds to interacting climatic, cryospheric, and anthropogenic drivers remain poorly constrained. Here, we integrated long-term multi-source Earth observation data to quantify the spatiotemporal trends of grassland gross primary productivity (GPP) across the TP from 1982 to 2018 and examined the relationships between GPP and snow dynamics, climate, and grazing intensity, with an explicit emphasis on elevation-dependent controls. Our results reveal a pronounced nonlinear reorganization of GPP controls along elevation gradients, with a critical transition zone at mid-elevations (∼3500–4000 m). Within this zone, warming exerted the strongest positive association with GPP, while grazing intensity also showed a positive spatial association with GPP. In contrast, at higher elevations (>4500 m), snow dynamics emerged as dominant constraints on GPP. Structural equation modeling further indicates that snow cover duration showed the strongest negative total effect among the modeled environmental variables, whereas grazing intensity showed an elevation – dependent association with GPP, shifting from a positive spatial correlation at mid – elevations to a negative correlation at high elevations. Across all elevation zones, soil moisture-mediated pathways consistently exert stronger controls on GPP than soil temperature pathways, highlighting water availability as the more direct and dominant constraint on alpine grassland productivity. These findings demonstrate that elevation fundamentally regulates the spatial organization of ecosystem productivity controls on the TP and underscore the importance of explicitly accounting for cryosphere–biosphere–human interactions when assessing alpine carbon dynamics under a warming and wetting climate.

title: Active CO2 lidar extends satellite monitoring of urban fossil-fuel CO2 emissions to high-aerosol cities
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Cities with high aerosol loading are critical yet underserved targets for satellite-based monitoring of urban fossil-fuel CO 2 (ffCO 2 ) emissions, because passive XCO 2 retrievals often suffer from severe data loss and aerosol-induced uncertainty under polluted conditions. Here, we evaluate whether spaceborne active CO 2 lidar can extend satellite carbon monitoring to such observationally challenging environments. We combine CO 2 observations from the DQ-1 Aerosol and Carbon Dioxide Lidar (ACDL) with Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI NO 2 retrievals to construct an active–passive framework. Near-synchronous ACDL–TROPOMI overpasses are used to derive city-specific ffCO 2 -to-NO x emission ratios, which are then applied to TROPOMI-derived daily NO x emissions to reconstruct observation-constrained ffCO 2 variability. Among the top 100 urban ffCO 2 emitters, high-AOD cities are concentrated in the Asia–Pacific region, and under polluted conditions, DQ-1 provides 201.6% and 107.8% more effective CO 2 observations than OCO-2 and OCO-3, respectively. Applications to six high-AOD cities in North China and India reveal physically interpretable seasonal variability, with monthly emission magnitudes broadly consistent with EDGAR and ODIAC inventories (r = 0.79–0.81). These results demonstrate that active CO 2 lidar, when combined with dense NO 2 observations, can provide an independent top-down constraint to support urban carbon monitoring and mitigation assessment in polluted cities where passive carbon satellites are most limited.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Foundation Models
Retrieval of nighttime oceanic liquid cloud optical and microphysical parameters from VIIRS observations: a physics-informed machine learning approach
Piecewise log-normal modeling of Sentinel-1 co-cross polarization coherence and application to wind field Bayesian inversion
abstract: Accurate estimates of kilometer-scale ocean surface wind fields is critical for many applications, including weather forecasting, marine navigation, offshore wind energy development, ... Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) plays a key role in retrieving wind speed by analyzing changes in sea surface roughness, described through Geophysical Model Functions (GMFs). However, the inverse problem of wind retrieval from SAR data is under-determined, requiring ancillary information from Numerical Weather Models (NWP) to resolve ambiguities in the wind direction. The Co-Cross-Polarization Coherence (CCPC) has recently emerged as a valuable SAR-derived observation for improving wind direction estimates. While an initial GMF for CCPC was introduced by \cite{10.1109/tgrs.2021.3055979}, it proved inadequate for high wind speeds. We present PGMF-2, a refined GMF for CCPC, ensuring reliable performance up to 30 m/s by modeling its wind speed components as log-normal functions. The need for crosstalk calibration is mitigated by a burst-based processing.Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the unique odd-symmetry of the CCPC and the different impact of the wind direction modulation on its real and imaginary parts complements the Normalized Radar Cross Section (NRCS) to estimate the wind direction. This combination enables wind direction retrieval without NWP priors, even outperforming NWP-based inversions between 7 and 15 m/s. The Mean Absolute Error on direction reaches as low as 25° in favorable high-wind conditions.A case study on Storm Alex (2020) serves as a proof of concept of the Bayesian scheme on real-world observations, successfully retrieving the typical flow organization of the cyclonic system without reliance on NWP priors.

title: Remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments: A critical review and integrated analysis of Lastarria volcano
abstract: Hydrothermal alteration is a key process in active volcanic systems, influencing edifice stability, fluid circulation, degassing pathways, and volcanic hazards. Remote sensing is widely used to map hydrothermal alteration; however, many approaches treat alteration-related surfaces as static targets, so their reliability, transferability, and process significance in active volcanic environments remain insufficiently evaluated. This study synthesizes commonly used remote sensing approaches and examines the behavior and interpretive implications of representative outputs at Lastarria volcano, which is an arid, high-altitude, vegetation-free system with active fumarolic fields. We compare visual interpretation, VNIR-SWIR reflectance products, pixel-based and sub-pixel mapping outputs, UAV thermal infrared observations, and LiDAR-derived surface-state information. The results show that visual interpretation, reflectance-based products, and pixel-based or sub-pixel outputs delineate broad alteration-related patterns, but their extent, internal structure, and interpretive meaning vary with methodological choices, surface mixing, and environmental surface states. Thermal infrared observations constrain apparent surface-temperature anomalies and fumarole-proximal activity, whereas LiDAR-derived products provide complementary information on surface state, morphology, and roughness. These observations do not converge on a single alteration representation; instead, they capture different aspects of the volcanic-hydrothermal system. Environmental, climatic, and surface controls, including exposure state, moisture, surface reworking, and seasonality, further limit direct transferability among volcanic settings. We suggest that remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments should move from deterministic mapping toward process-oriented and uncertainty-aware interpretation, with temporal persistence, spatial coherence, process plausibility, and independent support providing a basis for future multi-temporal analysis and monitoring.

title: DescribeEarth: Detailed localized captioning for remote sensing images
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Automated textual description of remote sensing images is crucial for unlocking their full potential in diverse applications, from environmental monitoring to urban planning and disaster management. However, existing studies in remote sensing image captioning primarily focus on the image level, lacking object-level fine-grained interpretation, which prevents the full utilization and transformation of the rich semantic and structural information contained in remote sensing images. Consequently, we propose Geo-DLC, a novel task for fine-grained object-level image captioning in remote sensing. To systematically establish and evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce a comprehensive suite encompassing a dataset, a benchmark, and a specialized model. Specifically, we construct DE-Dataset, a large-scale collection comprising 25 categories and 261,806 annotated instances with detailed descriptions of object attributes, relationships, and contexts. To provide a rigorous evaluation standard, we develop DE-Benchmark, an LLM-assisted evaluation protocol based on question answering, to accurately measure the capabilities of models on the Geo-DLC task. Furthermore, we present DescribeEarth, an MLLM architecture explicitly tailored for this task. It integrates a scale-adaptive focal strategy and a domain-guided fusion module, which leverage the features of remote sensing Vision-Language Model (VLM) to encode high-resolution details and category priors while maintaining the global context. Extensive evaluations show that DescribeEarth achieves the highest aggregate scores on the simple and complex subsets and matches GPT-4o on the out-of-distribution subset of DE-Benchmark. Its clearest gains occur in surrounding-context coverage and in categories whose interpretation depends strongly on overhead spatial layout and remote-sensing context. All data, code, and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/earth-insights/DescribeEarth .

title: 160 Years of Etna summit craters through a photogrammetry-based time machine
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: This study presents a quantitative, multi-temporal assessment of Etna’s summit morpho-structural evolution, spanning a 160-year (1865–2024) period. We integrated historical topographic maps with modern, high-resolution remote sensing data, including Unoccupied Aerial System surveys. Dataset-specific validation and statistical error propagation yielded root mean square errors ranging from decametric values for the earliest cartographic sources to metric values for the post-2020 datasets. The resulting topographic time series was interpreted alongside geological observations and previously published geodetic analyses. This integrated reconstruction documents the transition from a predominantly monocentric summit configuration to a highly dynamic polycentric system, and reveals contrasting morpho-structural behaviours among the four summit craters. VOR is characterized by recent constructive growth, BN and NEC by recurrent infilling followed by subsidence, whereas the SEC exhibits persistent constructive growth accompanied by progressive eastward expansion. These differences are consistent with variations in crater position, structural setting, shallow feeding-system configuration, and dominant eruptive style. The long-term evolution of the summit area is also consistent with the influence of the North-East and South Rift zones, and with published geodetic observations describing the seaward deformation of Etna’s eastern flank. Overall, the reconstructed evolution highlights the interaction between volcanic construction, structural controls, and gravitational deformation in shaping a continuously changing and asymmetric summit system. The proposed geospatial workflow provides a reproducible and transferable framework for integrating heterogeneous historical and modern topographic datasets and for investigating long-term morpho-structural change at other highly active volcanoes.

title: Atmospheric restoration is a prerequisite for sub-pixel fire mapping: A smoke-robust protocol across five fire regions
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Wildfires exert profound impacts on global ecosystems; however, accurate satellite-based burn area extraction is frequently confounded by the inherent mixed-pixel issue and complex atmospheric conditions. Although sub-pixel mapping (SPM) can resolve the mixed pixel issue, the extent to which its extraction accuracy depends on initial atmospheric preprocessing under diverse haze and smoke conditions remains poorly quantified. Furthermore, the conditions under which such preprocessing remains effective, and the boundary of its operational envelope, are not well understood. This study introduces a Smoke-Robust Sub-pixel Mapping (SRSPM) protocol to systematically diagnose atmospheric preprocessing efficacy prior to SPM. Using both simulated and real atmospheric states across five distinct fire regions, we systematically evaluate the sensitivity of sub-pixel fire perimeter delineation to different levels of haze contamination. Our findings demonstrate that atmospheric scattering inherently degrades the spatial allocation capabilities of SPM, leading to severe omission errors. Restoring contaminated spectral signals is shown to be essential, rather than merely beneficial, for accurate mapping when haze contamination is substantial. Crucially, our quantitative diagnosis reveals the operational limits of the SRSPM protocol: the dehazing benefit grows with haze intensity and remains substantial up to the strongest simulated contamination ( w = 1); in one region it turns positive only beyond w ≈0.73, delineating the quantitative envelope of the SRSPM protocol. Overall, this work establishes the SRSPM protocol as a practical diagnostic tool for quantifying the interaction between atmospheric correction and sub-pixel spatial allocation, providing empirical guidance for operational disaster monitoring in complex atmospheric environments.

title: Improving automatic glacier mapping accuracy, robustness, and reliability across the Third Pole Region
abstract: Most automatic glacier mapping methods applied in the Third Pole Region (TPR), exhibit suboptimal accuracy for debris-covered glaciers, high sensitivity to interferences, and large uncertainty in model outputs, thereby limiting their operational utility. These challenges can be mitigated by deploying advanced deep learning models and enhancing dataset representativeness across complex imaging conditions. Accordingly, we compiled three large-scale datasets used for model development, glacier-level mapping evaluation, and cross-sensor generalisation assessment, respectively. We then evaluated several state-of-the-art deep learning networks and found that the adapted TransUNet performed best. On the test dataset, the model achieves a glacier Intersection over Union (IoU) of 90% and 83% in patches featuring debris-free and debris-covered glaciers, respectively, while maintaining robust under challenging conditions. Glacier-level validation further confirms the effective detection of glacier counts and precise outlines, with both metrics improving with glacier area and the global IoUTPR > 80%. Uncertainty quantification shows high output reliability, with expected calibration errors of 0.029 and 0.009 for the test and glacier-level test datasets, respectively. Our fully automated 2024–2025 Karakoram glacier inventory, comprising 12,981 glaciers covering a total area of ~19,484 km2, exhibits high agreement with earlier inventories and reflects current glacier state. The primary contribution of this study is the development of a scalable framework that, by optimising dataset representativeness and algorithmic architectures, significantly elevates the accuracy, robustness, reliability and operational value of glacier mapping across the TPR.

title: Guest Editors’ Introduction: Special Section on Computational Photography (ICCP)
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence

title: WISE: A lightweight, weakly-supervised model for onboard fire smoke detection and localization
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Wildfire smoke detection from satellite imagery is critical for early warning and rapid response. For onboard satellite deployment, detection systems must operate under strict memory and latency constraints while providing spatially informative outputs for downstream decision-making. Existing tile-level classification methods are computationally efficient but lack spatial localization, whereas pixel-level segmentation approaches provide detailed masks yet are typically too computationally demanding for real-time onboard execution. To address this gap, we propose WISE (Weakly-supervised Inference-efficient Smoke Extraction), a deployment-oriented framework for onboard fire smoke detection and localization. WISE leverages only tile-level annotations through a teacher–student distillation strategy, where an offline teacher provides soft spatial supervision to a lightweight WISE-Student optimized for efficient onboard inference. The student jointly predicts tile-level smoke presence and smoke probability maps within a single forward pass, enabling spatially informative detection under strict computational constraints. WISE was evaluated through in-orbit execution aboard the ISS-mounted IMAGIN-e payload. Three model variants achieve average inference times of 0.10 s, 0.14 s, and 0.26 s per tile, indicating near-real-time per-tile inference within onboard resource limits. Ground-based experiments on Landsat 5 and Landsat 8 imagery further indicate effective detection and spatially informative localization. The best-performing variant achieves a mean tile-level F1 score of 0.964 and a mean pixel-level F1 score of 0.750 across 10 runs, while containing only 0.12M parameters and requiring approximately 3 GFLOPs. Together, these results indicate that WISE is a practical candidate for low-latency wildfire smoke monitoring from space under onboard resource constraints.

title: Evolving transformers with reinforcement learning-enhanced Grey Wolf Optimisation for remote sensing image segmentation
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Semantic segmentation of remote sensing images (RSI) faces various challenges due to the presence of multi-scale objects with high intra-class and low inter-class variations. Existing models often show limited robustness in tackling diverse remote sensing benchmarks and modalities under closed-set settings. To address the above challenges, we propose a new Grey Wolf Optimisation (GWO) variant-optimised encoder architecture, a new Gaussian-enhanced self-attention strategy and a gradient-guided Convolutional Block Attention Module (GGCBAM), to adapt to different segmentation tasks under closed-set settings effectively. Specifically, informed by loss gradients, GGCBAM is able to identify channel/spatial features not only important but also critical to prediction. The new self-attention variant utilises a Gaussian distribution-based bias to better emphasise local details. Hybrid attention strategies by stacking GGCBAM and Gaussian-enhanced self-attention methods in two opposite sequential orders are constructed. The proposed GWO algorithm is used to optimise the numbers of these hybrid attention blocks and their fusion weights in the dual-branch encoder for dynamic architecture generation. This new GWO variant employs 3D geometric shapes and deep reinforcement learning algorithms, i.e. Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C), for hybrid leader construction and search action selection, respectively, to increase search diversity. As indicated in empirical studies, our optimised network effectively extracts important global spatial context while preserving vital fine-grained local structures, and outperforms a number of state-of-the-art transformer networks for solving diverse segmentation tasks.

title: A multi-sensor and multi-temporal GeoAI framework for resolving ecological scale mismatch in Antarctica
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Advances in remote sensing (RS) and artificial intelligence (AI) are enabling new approaches to ecological monitoring across spatial and temporal scales. However, vegetation mapping in polar environments remains constrained by a fundamental mismatch between the fine spatial scale of ecological processes and the coarse resolution of satellite observations, as well as by limited availability of biologically reliable training data. In this study, we address these challenges by developing an end-to-end GeoAI framework that integrates field observations, drone imagery, and satellite time-series data to enable cross-scale vegetation mapping. We propose a progressive weak-to-strong labelling workflow that begins with 1) biologically grounded quadrat annotations, to create iteratively expanded training data along with 2) spectral similarity combined with machine learning, followed by 3) training with deep learning (DL) models for pixel-level segmentation. Native Sentinel-2 observations (10–20 m spatial resolution) were processed using DL-based super-resolution to an approximately 1 m output grid. High-resolution drone DL predictions were subsequently transformed into fractional cover labels aligned to the super-resolved satellite grid, supporting cross-scale modelling across centimetre-to-metre resolutions. We evaluate multiple DL architectures using spatially separated UAV evaluation data and assess satellite-scale performance as agreement with UAV-derived fractional cover reference labels. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves the scalability and ecological relevance of vegetation mapping in data-limited environments. The best-performing drone-scale DL model (DeepLabv3+) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.91 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.85 for fine-scale vegetation segmentation. At the satellite scale, the U-Net fractional-cover model achieved strong predictive performance for dominant vegetation classes, including cyanobacteria (R 2 = 0.94) and red Hennediella heimii moss (R 2 = 0.88), with reduced performance for spectrally complex or sparsely represented classes, demonstrating effective cross-scale vegetation mapping despite challenges associated with sub-pixel heterogeneity and spectral mixing. This study provides a generalisable methodological framework for integrating multi-sensor data and AI in ecological RS, demonstrating strong cross-scale performance while illustrating the challenges of capturing fine-scale vegetation heterogeneity at satellite scales.

title: Extending ocean color product to three dimensions assisted by high spectral resolution lidar data
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Satellite ocean color remote sensing has revolutionized our understanding of global marine ecosystems, but remains fundamentally limited to two-dimensional (2D) observations. To address this limitation, we propose a Depth-Resolved Generalized Inherent Optical Property (DR-GIOP) model that merges passive multispectral remote sensing reflectance ( R rs ) from MODIS-Aqua with active depth-resolved particulate backscattering profiles ( b bp ) from High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL). Using lidar derived b bp ( z ) at a single wavelength and ocean color sensor derived spectral R rs ( λ ) as inputs, the model solves for depth-resolved spectral non-water absorption a pg ( z , λ ), particulate backscattering b bp ( z , λ ), and chlorophyll-a concentration Chl ( z ). We validated this model using coincident MODIS, airborne HSRL, and shipborne in-situ measurements from the SABOR campaign and three NAAMES campaigns. The results demonstrate that DR-GIOP successfully reconstructs reasonable three-dimensional (3D) optical structures, achieving the correlation coefficient r =∼0.85 for a pg ( z , λ ), b bp ( z , λ ), and Chl ( z ).Comparative analysis indicates that DR-GIOP significantly outperforms traditional 2D models such as Seeded GIOP, GIOP-DC, and QAA. Furthermore, we quantitatively analyze the shallow-layer bias of passive 2D remote sensing and demonstrate how active–passive fusion effectively mitigates this bias. This study proposes a promising framework for 3D ocean color reconstruction, offering new insights for future multi-sensor satellite missions. In the future, we can envision the realization of a satellite that carries an advanced HSRL and multi-spectral sensors, providing high accuracy of b bp ( z ) and R rs ( λ ) and promising 3D ocean subsurface observations at a global scale.

title: Bridging cloud-induced gaps in MODIS leaf area index products using high-frequency geostationary satellite observations
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a fundamental variable for characterizing vegetation canopy structure and ecosystem functioning. However, persistent cloud contamination substantially constrains the spatiotemporal continuity of LAI products derived from polar-orbiting satellite observations. In contrast, geostationary satellites provide dense temporal sampling, offering a valuable observational basis for filling data gaps in polar-orbiting satellite products. To bridge this observational gap, this study develops an observation-complementary framework that integrates high-frequency Himawari-8 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI) observations with MODIS LAI products to achieve LAI reconstruction in cloud-prone regions. Within this framework, AHI observations are first used to retrieve LAI at a spatial resolution of 2 km using a Random Forest model trained with a high-quality MODIS-based benchmark dataset, and are then downscaled to 500 m using MODIS-derived spatial texture information. The reconstructed AHI LAI is subsequently integrated into low-quality or missing MODIS pixels to generate a fused AHI-MODIS LAI dataset over China. Validation against in-situ measurements and cross-comparison results show that the fused product maintains reasonable numerical consistency and stable temporal trajectories. Data availability increases from 70.70% to 90.90% under the 4-day compositing cycle. These results indicate that geostationary-polar-orbiting observation complementarity provides a practical pathway for improving the continuity and usability of optical LAI products in persistently cloudy regions, while remaining subject to the constraints of optical observations and cross-scale reconstruction assumptions.

title: BD-Diff: Generative Diffusion Model for Image Deblurring on Unknown Domains with Blur-Decoupled Learning
TAME-MA: Taming Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Level Trustworthiness Under Jailbreak Manipulations
PosePAL: Efficient Animal Pose Labeling Using Point Trackers
abstract: Abstract Automatically estimating animal poses from videos is important for studying animal behavior. Existing methods do not perform reliably, partly because they rely on high-quality training data, and existing such datasets are small. It is challenging and expensive to create such data, due to the large variations in animal morphology and the difficulty of frame-wise video annotation in general. In this paper, we introduce an animal pose labeling pipeline that leverages test-time optimization of a point tracker, providing temporally-consistent annotations at low cost. Given a video, we fine-tune a lightweight appearance embedding inside a pre-trained general-purpose point tracker on a sparse set of annotated frames. These annotations can be obtained from human labelers or off-the-shelf pose detectors. The fine-tuned model is then applied to the rest of the frames for automatic labeling. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance at a reasonable annotation cost. We believe our pipeline offers a valuable tool for the automatic quantification of animal behavior. Visit our project webpage at https://zhuoyang-pan.github.io/animal-labeling .

title: Voxelized 3D Gaussian Representation for Dense Visual SLAM on Embedded Vision System
Pseudo-label Refinement and Model-State Recovery for Continual Test-Time Adaptation on Semantic Segmentation
Sampling-Free Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection with Synergistic Optimization Alignment
abstract: Abstract Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection (UniDAOD) addresses domain shifts in open-world scenarios without assuming pre-defined shared categories between source and target domains. Despite progress in this field, existing methods rely heavily on thresholding techniques to filter private category samples, which introduces challenges in hyperparameter tuning and handling noisy data. To overcome these limitations, we propose Synergistic Optimization Alignment (SOA), a sampling-free framework that tackles two challenges inherent in UniDAOD: multi-scale discriminator discrepancy and task-dominant gradient conflict. To address the discrepancy among multi-scale discriminators, we propose Multi-Scale Discriminator Alignment (MDA) to adaptively aggregate under-aligned discriminators for shared classes, ensuring consistent feature alignment across scales. To address task-dominant gradient conflicts, we propose Gradient Coordinated Optimization (GCO), which suppresses conflicting domain-alignment gradients and coordinates their magnitudes to prevent domain over-alignment, thereby mitigating private-class interference while preserving beneficial domain-invariant supervision. Extensive experiments on open-set, partial-set, and closed-set domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that SOA outperforms state-of-the-art UniDAOD and DAOD methods. Code is available at https://github.com/zyfone/SOA .

title: Nested generative downscaling of passive microwave satellite data for navigation-scale Arctic sea ice forecasting
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Rapid Arctic sea ice decline is increasing the accessibility of high-latitude shipping routes, but route-scale planning remains limited by the spatial resolution and ice-edge accuracy of Arctic sea ice concentration (SIC) forecasts. Coarse forecast products can smooth marginal ice zones, narrow straits, and fine-scale ice-edge features that are important for identifying navigable corridors during seasonal melt and freeze-up. Here we introduce IceNest, a navigation-oriented Arctic SIC forecasting framework that generates daily 6.25 km SIC forecasts up to 30 days ahead. IceNest couples a deep learning-based 25 km pan-Arctic forecast ensemble with a conditional diffusion model for residual downscaling. The forecasting ensemble uses the long OSI SAF SSM/I(S) passive microwave record together with historical environmental variables from ERA5, while the downscaling model learns AMSR-scale residual corrections from AMSR-series observations. Across 2020–2023, IceNest outperformed damped persistence and the evaluated Copernicus Climate Change Service seasonal forecast systems in terms of binary accuracy and integrated ice-edge error, with the largest gains during summer melt and autumn freeze-up. Route simulations along the Northeast Passage further yielded smaller errors in navigable-window timing and route distance than GloSea5/6 when evaluated against an AMSR2-based reference, highlighting the framework’s relevance to Arctic transit planning.

title: HELIOS-Net: Hourly daytime estimation of land surface temperature with integration of observational solar-cloud-satellite geometry and deep neural network
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Geostationary satellite-based land surface temperature (LST) is vital for monitoring diurnal thermal dynamics owing to its extensive spatial coverage and high temporal resolution. However, frequent cloud cover results in substantial data gaps, limiting its practical utility for reliable thermal monitoring applications. The solar-cloud-satellite geometry (SCSG) effect has recently been introduced to reflect direct cloud radiative effects in LST reconstruction, but its application has been largely limited to polar-orbiting satellites. To address this limitation, we propose HELIOS-Net, a deep learning (DL) framework for hourly daytime LST reconstruction using the GEO-KOMPSAT-2A satellite across South Korea, central Japan, and southeastern Australia. The framework combines SCSG-based regime partitioning with a generative adversarial network (GAN) to reconstruct spatially continuous all-sky LST by leveraging satellite observations and various meteorological and topographic variables. Validation against in-situ observations demonstrated that HELIOS-Net achieved high performance across all regions, with coefficient of determination (R 2 ) values of 0.63–0.94 and root mean square error (RMSE) values of 2.45–7.65 °C under cloudy-sky conditions. Comparative evaluation further indicated an overall performance advantage over ERA5-Land and an existing all-sky LST product derived from satellite observations. Additional analyses confirmed that both the SCSG effect and the DL framework contribute to enhancing the fidelity of hourly daytime LST reconstruction. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework to enable high-quality, spatially continuous all-sky LST monitoring from geostationary satellites, providing a promising approach mitigating cloud-induced data gaps under diverse viewing geometries and environmental conditions.

title: PatchFusion: Resilient LiDAR-camera fusion for point cloud semantic segmentation in autonomous driving
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: LiDAR-camera fusion for point cloud semantic segmentation is essential for accurate and reliable 3D perception of autonomous driving systems. Contemporary LiDAR-camera fusion approaches predominantly integrate the pixel-level camera features located by projected points to augment the corresponding 3D points, which can be abstractly defined as point-pixel fusion strategy. Although such point-pixel fusion mode has been proved to be effective and widely used in practice, the strategy has two non-ignorable defects: (1) dependent on precise point-pixel projection correspondence, (2) limited by just using extremely little image information. Besides, the LiDAR-only inference in offline fusion fails to utilize the synchronously obtained images to achieve a dynamic fusion for 3D perception, while LiDAR-camera fusion inference in online fusion still encounters challenges of field of view (FoV) discrepancy between sensors. Moreover, the corruption robustness of LiDAR-camera fusion methods for 3D semantic segmentation, a crucial factor for the practical reliability of perception systems, has received limited attention. Thus, focusing on addressing above challenges, we develop the point-patch fusion mode, and construct PatchFusion framework as a systematic and promising solution to enhance performance and resilience of LiDAR-camera fusion perception in realistic and complex driving scenes. Specifically, in PatchFusion, we propose to leverage cross-attention mechanism to implement high-quality point-patch fusion by automatically searching what information should be highlighted or suppressed from the local patch of image, thereby alleviating the adverse effects of projection errors, maximizing the utilization of the high-density image information, and being more robust to the potential image corruptions. Besides, we integrate the strengths of offline and online fusion modes and propose a bidirectional cross-modality knowledge distillation strategy, aiming to further enhance the performance and robustness for predictions within and outside camera FoV. Finally, to bridge the research gap regarding the corruption robustness of LiDAR-camera fusion methods, we design a specialized dataset corruption suite for public multimodal datasets to simulate complex evaluation conditions by synthesizing projection noises and image corruptions. Extensive experiments on well-known datasets in autonomous driving (SemanticKITTI and nuScenes) demonstrate that PatchFusion can effectively improve the performance and resilience of LiDAR-camera fusion for 3D semantic segmentation on both clean and corrupted datasets. The relevant code will be available at https://github.com/sssssyf/PatchFusion .

title: SNAIL-Radar-Indoor:A large-scale handheld LiDAR–4D radar–IMU dataset for robust SLAM in degraded environments
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Multimodal sensing, particularly 4D imaging radar, is promising for emergency search and rescue because it remains informative under smoke and highly reflective structures. However, existing public radar datasets predominantly record outdoor vehicle motion or clean indoor spaces. We present SNAIL-Radar-Indoor, a large-scale handheld LiDAR–4D radar–IMU dataset for SLAM in smoke and other degraded environments. Extending our previous outdoor SNAIL-Radar benchmark, the new release contains 217 sequences totaling approximately 850 min, collected at 13 sites across six scene types, including offices, abandoned buildings, halls, factory workshops, underground parking areas, and connecting outdoor spaces. The sequences cover corridors, rooms, staircases, narrow corners, indoor–outdoor transitions, reflective structures, dynamic crowds, and real smoke. Data were recorded using a compact self-developed integrated platform comprising a 3D LiDAR, a low-cost single-chip 4D imaging radar, a consumer-grade IMU, and an optional barometer. Repeated traversals and closed paths are included where feasible to support place recognition and loop-closure evaluation. The released trajectories are method-generated references and do not constitute independent absolute ground truth. Smoke-free sequences mainly use loop-consistent LIO references; fully smoke-dominated sequences use an iRIOM-based radar–IMU reference with AHRS and barometer constraints; and partially degraded sequences use a smoke-aware piecewise RLIO reference. Closed sequences additionally include start–end LiDAR registration constraints, while non-closed sequences are accompanied by map-based end-to-end displacement checks. The dataset supports research on radar and multimodal registration, smoke-robust odometry and mapping, denoising, environmental perception, and navigation in degraded environments.

title: SaKD: Lightweight infrared small target detection via Spatial-Aware Knowledge Distillation for edge deployment
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate infrared small target detection (IRSTD) in remote sensing remains challenging because targets of interest typically occupy only a few pixels and provide limited spatial cues against complex backgrounds. Existing high-performance methods rely on complex networks to enhance weak target representations, limiting their use on resource-constrained edge devices. Lightweight models reduce computation but struggle to capture scarce spatial cues of small targets. To preserve these spatial cues in lightweight models for remote sensing applications, we propose SaKD, a Spatial-Aware Knowledge Distillation method for IRSTD. SaKD explicitly captures complementary spatial cues associated with target responses from teacher predictions, thereby providing richer spatial discriminative supervision for the student model. Without changing the student inference structure, SaKD introduces two training stage components. The Multi-Scale Self Guidance Mechanism first derives auxiliary supervision from the student’s own responses at multiple scales to strengthen target representation before teacher guidance is introduced. Spatial Prior Distillation then transfers the teacher’s spatial priors by enforcing region, position, and scale consistency, corresponding to target region coverage, center localization, and response scale control. Experiments on multiple IRSTD datasets containing real remote sensing imagery show that SaKD consistently improves the undistilled lightweight student and achieves competitive detection performance with low model complexity. The distilled student contains only 0.895M parameters and 1.999G FLOPs. Deployment verification on a Jetson platform further demonstrates its practical efficiency for edge deployable remote sensing applications, reaching 142.7 FPS for standalone TensorRT FP16 inference at an input resolution of 256 × 256. The code will be available at: https://github.com/Kingwin97/SaKD .
concepts: Enhanced Data Rates for GSM Evolution

title: Resampling-free jitter-aware bundle adjustment for HiRISE multi-CCD stereo mapping on Mars
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate topographic reconstruction from High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) stereo imagery is essential for Martian geomorphological analysis and landing-site assessment. However, high-frequency sensor jitter and geometric inconsistency among non-collinear charge-coupled devices (CCDs) can introduce seam-related artifacts, periodic residuals, and local digital elevation model (DEM) deformation. Conventional correction workflows often estimate jitter in image space or update attitude parameters before stereo measurement, and therefore do not fully exploit the internal overlap constraints of the HiRISE focal plane within bundle adjustment. This paper presents a resampling-free photogrammetric framework for HiRISE multi-CCD stereo mapping, in which harmonic jitter compensation is embedded directly into rigorous bundle adjustment. A time-continuous exterior orientation model combines low-order polynomial motion with Fourier-series-based jitter terms initialized from adjacent-CCD overlap disparities. Inter-orbit stereo tie points and inter-CCD overlap tie points are then jointly used to constrain stereo geometry, time-dependent pointing variation, and focal-plane consistency in a unified adjustment model. For original CCD-image matching, a constrained coarse-to-fine pipeline is developed. Pretrained XFeat with test-time descriptor adaptation is used mainly for prior-free coarse initialization at the lowest pyramid level, and the resulting geometric relation is propagated to guide efficient Harris + normalized cross-correlation (NCC) refinement and dense grid matching under local constraints. Experiments on four HiRISE stereo pairs covering the Spirit landing region, Mawrth Vallis, the Zhurong landing region, and a more topographically challenging inverted-channel area in Gale Crater are used to evaluate the proposed framework under different terrain-relief conditions. The results show that the proposed framework maintains sub-pixel mean check-point reprojection residuals in both image directions across all four stereo pairs, suppresses jitter-induced periodic residuals, improves consistency across CCD seams, and produces DEMs consistent with the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) and official HiRISE/Planetary Data System (PDS) references without image resampling. The implementation will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/wbl1997/mars_images_ba.git .

title: Enhanced early warning of extreme river discharge events in the Yangtze River Basin using atmospheric circulation signals
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Early warning of extreme river discharge events (ERDEs) is crucial for water resources management and disaster reduction in the Yangtze River Basin (YRB), yet substantial uncertainty remains in their prediction. This study proposes a novel strategy to enhance ERDE early warning by detecting its associated atmospheric circulation signals. We develop DetRF, a machine learning model that integrates anomaly detection with a balanced random forest ensemble. DetRF was trained and validated using ERA5 reanalysis data from 2000 to 2019 and independently applied to 2020–2024, with its early warning performance evaluated against satellite-based precipitation and reanalysis river discharge data. Across eight subregions of the YRB, DetRF effectively detects ERDE-related atmospheric circulation signals, achieving mean recall, precision, and F1 score values of 0.756, 0.506, and 0.576, respectively, and consistently outperforming benchmark machine learning models. The detected signals accurately capture key synoptic features associated with hydrological extremes, including the positions and intensities of troughs, vortices, and cyclones, as well as moisture transport. More than 99% of the detected signals are followed by precipitation within five days, while persistent precipitation occurs in over 67% of cases across both local and upstream regions. More importantly, an average of 93.8% of DetRF-detected circulation signals are followed by at least one ERDE within the subsequent five days. These findings establish a direct link between specific atmospheric circulation signals and subsequent hydrological extremes, offering a new pathway for extending ERDE early warning beyond conventional hydrological prediction. The proposed framework is particularly promising for regions where hydrological observations are sparse.

title: Estimating supraglacial lake bottom ablation rates by integrating ICESat-2 repeat track data and multi-temporal sentinel-2 imagery
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Supraglacial lakes are widely distributed across the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) each summer. The resulting meltwater-enhanced ablation effect plays a critical role in understanding the GrIS surface mass balance but remains poorly quantified. Inspired by the insight that longer meltwater persistence leads to stronger meltwater-enhanced ablation, this study proposes a novel method to directly estimate supraglacial lake bottom ablation rates at centimeter-per-day scale using satellite observations. First, we map multi-temporal supraglacial lake extents from Sentinel-2 imagery to estimate cumulative meltwater-covered days. Then, we derive ablation depths at the lake bottom and surrounding bare ice by differencing ICESat-2 repeat track data acquired before and during the melt season. Next, we perform linear fitting between lake bottom ablation depths and cumulative meltwater-covered days along the ICESat-2 tracks to calculate both the lake bottom ablation rate and the bare ice ablation rate. Finally, we evaluate the magnitude of the meltwater-enhanced ablation effect. We apply this method to 26 supraglacial lakes across the GrIS and identify a positive linear relationship between lake bottom ablation depths and cumulative water-covered days (mean Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.70 ± 0.14, p < 0.001). The fitted mean lake bottom ablation rate (4.50 ± 1.15 cm/day) significantly exceeds the mean bare ice ablation rate (1.98 ± 0.52 cm/day). Meltwater in supraglacial lakes therefore enhances ablation rate by ∼ 1.3 ± 0.5 times, with values ranging from 0.6 to 2.4, consistent with previous field measurements (1.1–1.4 times) and numerical model simulations (1.1–1.7 times). In summary, this study provides a first quantitative satellite-based estimate of meltwater-enhanced ablation across the GrIS under varying ablation intensities, and may improve our understanding of GrIS surface melt process.

title: Analysis of intraday urban thermal anisotropy and downward shortwave radiation through UAV experiment and coupled model
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The pronounced thermal radiation anisotropy observed in rapidly urbanizing areas arises from the complex interplay of solar downward shortwave radiation (DSWR), building geometry, and local topography. To address this, we propose a novel framework, termed GRay-AU3SM-IRT, for the analysis of urban thermal anisotropy (UTA). The study was conducted in a representative mountainous city in Chongqing, China. A specific 0.4 × 0.4 km 2 area, characterized by buildings and terrain on 10° slopes, was selected for analysis at hourly resolution. The simulations showed strong agreement with measured data, achieving a root mean square error below 0.46 K and a coefficient of determination exceeding 0.79. The analysis reveals that UTA shows pronounced diurnal variations: it intensifies gradually in the morning, peaks at solar noon with clear hotspot formation, and generates secondary hotspots in the afternoon due to changing solar azimuth and slope effects. The morning striped distribution pattern caused by building geometry diminishes with declining solar irradiance and disappears by afternoon. Diurnal trends in the UTA Effect (UTAE), directional brightness temperature (DBT), DBT Effect (DBTE), and DSWR are generally aligned. Notably, UTAE and DBTE peak before DSWR, while both maximum and minimum DBT peak later. The proposed framework offers key advantages: precise multi-lap UAV navigation, minimized motion artifacts, consistent temporal sampling via adaptive velocity control, gap-filling through simulation, and spatio-temporal outlier correction. It provides critical data for angle normalization and correction across diverse urban environments.

title: Remote-sensing-assisted and in situ-constrained reconstruction of 4-hourly chlorophyll-a dynamics in inland lakes using vision Mamba and temporal attention
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Chlorophyll a (Chl-a) is widely used to indicate eutrophication and bloom risk in inland waters, but daily Sentinel-3 observations alone cannot resolve transient sub-daily variability represented in partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a records. This study therefore develops VGTA (Vision Mamba–GKOA–TCN-Attention), a staged remote-sensing-assisted and in situ-constrained framework that integrates daily Sentinel-3 OLCI-derived priors with partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a sequences and binary observation masks. A 20-dimensional OLCI-derived feature space provides spectral–spatial priors for Chl-a estimation and bloom-risk state identification. GKOA optimizes TCN-Attention to reconstruct masked values within partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a sequences. Vision Mamba outperformed CNN– and Transformer-based models in Chl-a estimation, achieving 94.8% accuracy, a Macro-F1 score of 0.909, and a Bloom-F1 score of 0.870. Ablation experiments confirmed the contributions of bidirectional contextual modeling, positional embedding, selective state-space modeling, and gating. Under Missing Completely at Random, block-missing, and real missing scenarios, GTA improved reconstruction performance by 12.71–55.54% relative to the best baseline models. Uncertainty increased once continuous gaps reached seven days, defining a practical boundary of data-driven reconstruction. Chl-a fluctuations and bloom-risk transitions can unfold within a day, and daily satellite snapshots may blur their timing or miss short events. Reconstruction of masked time steps within partially observed 4-hourly in situ Chl-a sequences can support earlier identification of bloom-risk transitions, more timely field sampling and management responses, and temporally finer monitoring of inland waters.

title: Reference-anchored envelope modelling for predicting tree mortality hotspots driven by drought
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Predicting tree mortality hotspots driven by drought remains challenging, since vulnerability to drought is strongly influenced by climate, landform, and substrate. We propose a novel reference-anchored, quantile-envelope susceptibility model-implemented through a reproducible workflow- that exports mortality-resemblance (high-risk) environments from three confirmed tree-mortality footprints (training AOIs), based on semi-arid conifer and evergreen sclerophyllous forests in Cyprus, to produce wide screening layers. The approach combines (i) physiographic similarity derived from AOI-calibrated envelopes for slope, multi-scale topographic position and curvature (broad quantiles; majority-rule), (ii) exposure constraints via circular aspect windows, warm-season solar loading (April-September) and substrate (lithology) filtering, (iii) a drought severity gate (SPEI-12 (Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index-12) ≤ -1.4), and (iv) Landsat event-year spectral collapse relative to a fixed 3-year pre-event baseline, coupled with a year + 1 persistence rule to suppress transient stress. Our within-AOI evaluation (forest-only) showed substantial representativeness (coverage 70.49–85.35%), while recovering most reference mortality pixels (recall 67.62–100%). In 2025, two independent mortality sites were identified in Cyprus, coinciding with exceptional drought (SPEI < -2) and a sharp decline in the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) consistent with foliage browning, and occurring within high-risk zones as mapped in the final risk map. As a plausibility check, both 2025 sites fell within pre-mapped high-risk zones, with 83.50% and 82.69% of their forested area exceeding HEAT ≥ 0.60 and mean risk scores of 84.91% and 75.55%, respectively. With 18.88% of Cyprus’s total forest flagged as high-risk, the probability of this co-occurrence being random is p ≈ 0.036 (binomial test). Anchoring calibration to local mortality footprints makes the approach readily transferable to other regions with documented events.

title: A Targeted–Refined Framework for wind turbine detection integrating AlphaEarth Foundations and high-resolution multispectral satellite imagery
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The rapid expansion of clean energy systems, particularly wind and solar power, has made large-scale monitoring of related infrastructure using high-resolution multispectral satellite imagery increasingly important yet challenging. Conventional wind turbine detection approaches rely on pixel-level analysis of high-resolution imagery or sliding-window strategies. These methods often suffer from computational redundancy, low efficiency, and high false-positive rates, making them inadequate for supporting large-area surveys and operational monitoring. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Targeted–Refined framework based on AlphaEarth Foundations. First, a wind turbine sample database was constructed for model training and evaluation in Tianjin. In the Targeted Candidate Screening stage, a lightweight multi-layer perceptron classifier exploits the geospatial representations provided by AEF, enabling rapid identification of candidate regions while reducing the search space to approximately 5% of the original image patches. In the Refined Detection stage, high-resolution Jilin-1 satellite imagery is incorporated, and a YOLO model performs precise detection within the candidate regions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves a recall of 96.85%, a precision of 98.41%, and an F1-score of 97.63% on the Tianjin test set. Furthermore, the trained model is directly applied to the plains of the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region (excluding Tianjin) for cross-regional evaluation, where it identifies 1,580 wind turbines with an F1-score of 91.33%, demonstrating strong generalization capability. Overall, this framework provides an efficient and scalable solution for detecting large-scale, spatially sparse objects, and offers a practical approach for infrastructure inventory and monitoring of wind farms and similar assets.

title: Multi-angular assessment of early-season defoliation: Evaluating the sensitivity of vegetation indices to NPV visibility in temperate broadleaved forests
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Early-season forest decline in temperate broadleaved stands often lacks detectable biochemical stress signals, manifesting primarily through reduced foliage density and increased visibility of non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV). This study investigated the spectral separability of green leaves and NPV components under varying levels of canopy defoliation. Using a crane platform, we collected in situ leaf- and canopy-level spectrometer measurements alongside co-aligned photography to quantify the visible fraction of NPV. We analyzed the multi-angular reflectance characteristics and evaluated 35 vegetation indices (VIs) —including green biomass metrics and specialized NPV indices —using Random Forest to identify optimal spectral and geometric configurations. Sunlit young foliage exhibited high forward scatter, creating a nadir reflectance minimum. At canopy level, a nadir minimum was driven by the gap distribution resulting from sustainable forest management practices. Consequently, the optimal viewing angle for top-ranking VIs (e.g., SNC BAO , Ctr 2 , mNDVI 705 ) was near the hotspot geometry, minimizing shadowing and forest floor interference. While the total visible fraction of NPV remained mostly insensitive to viewing angles, its shaded proportion varied. VIs targeting green vegetation via red-edge and NIR domains consistently outperformed dedicated NPV indices based on SWIR cellulose and lignin absorption. This is attributed to low upper-canopy SWIR transmittance, which obscured the signals of the largely shaded NPV fraction. Top-performing VIs achieved R 2 = 0.92 for NPV visibility prediction, improving by 21 % over the best SWIR indices and 11 % over the nadir view. To accurately detect initial defoliation and overcome forest floor interference, adopting off-nadir viewing geometries is advantageous for capturing the optimal signal.

title: Unsupervised soft-min fusion of multi-sensor turbidity products using Gaussian mixture models
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Turbidity is a key indicator of water quality and particulate dynamics, making its accurate monitoring essential for aquatic ecosystem management. While satellite remote sensing enables large-scale turbidity observation, products derived from different sensors often exhibit inconsistencies due to differences in spectral responses, residual atmospheric effects, and viewing geometries. Effectively integrating such multi-source data in the absence of ground truth remains a significant challenge. Here, we propose Gaussian mixture model-based soft-min (GMMS), a fully unsupervised fusion framework in which neither model construction nor weight estimation relies on ground-truth turbidity observations. GMMS integrates Gaussian mixture modeling with a soft-min weighting strategy to identify latent error-structure contexts and adaptively assign sensor weights according to relative residual stability. By exploiting inter-sensor error characteristics, the framework enables context-aware data fusion. At the overall scale, GMMS significantly outperforms triple collocation (TC) and extended triple collocation for maximized correlation (ETCC) ( p < 0.05). Compared with in situ turbidity observations, GMMS increases the correlation coefficient from 0.798 to 0.841 and reduces the RMSE from 16.849 to 15.921 TU. Site-level evaluations further indicate enhanced robustness and reduced performance variability across monitoring stations. Simulation experiments confirm that GMMS achieves the greatest and most stable performance gains under conditions of moderate-to-high error-structure separability. Overall, GMMS provides an interpretable and transferable unsupervised fusion framework for improving multi-source satellite-derived turbidity estimates in complex riverine environments.

title: Expert knowledge-guided decision calibration for accurate fine-grained tree species classification
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate fine-grained tree species classification is critical for forest inventory and biodiversity monitoring. Existing methods predominantly focus on designing complex architectures to fit local data distributions. However, they often overlook the long-tailed distributions and high inter-class similarity inherent in limited data, thereby struggling to distinguish between few-shot or confusing categories. In the process of knowledge dissemination in the human world, individuals will actively seek expert assistance to transcend the limitations of local thinking. Inspired by this, we introduce an external ”Domain Expert” and propose an Expert Knowledge-Guided Classification Decision Calibration Network (EKDC-Net) to overcome these challenges. Our framework addresses two core issues: expert knowledge extraction and utilization. Specifically, we first develop a Local Prior Guided Knowledge Extraction Module (LPKEM). By leveraging Class Activation Map (CAM) analysis, LPKEM guides the domain expert to focus exclusively on discriminative features essential for classification. Subsequently, to effectively integrate this knowledge, we design an Uncertainty-Guided Decision Calibration Module (UDCM). This module dynamically corrects the local model’s decisions by considering both overall category uncertainty and instance-level prediction uncertainty. Furthermore, we present a large-scale classification dataset covering 102 tree species, named CU-Tree102 to address the issue of scarce diversity in current benchmarks. Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. Crucially, as a lightweight plug-and-play module, EKDC-Net improves backbone accuracy by 7.86% and precision by 12.89% using only 0.08M additional learnable parameters. The dataset, code, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/TreeCLS .

title: Kinematic pattern interpretation of railway-corridor deformation from InSAR time series with transfer learning-based TCN
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Railway-corridor deformation monitoring requires timely identification of localized displacement anomalies and characterization of their temporal evolution. Time-series Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides spatially dense and high-precision displacement observations from repeated SAR acquisitions, but InSAR-based railway studies have largely remained rate-centered, leaving the kinematic information embedded in displacement time series insufficiently exploited. This study develops a kinematic interpretation framework that integrates InSAR displacement time series, transfer learning-based Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) classification, and multi-source environmental data to characterize railway-corridor deformation in terms of its occurrence, temporal evolution, and environmental context. Sentinel-1 images acquired from January 2022 to December 2024 were processed to retrieve LOS displacement rates and displacement time series along the Kunming–Yuxi section of the China–Laos Railway. To reduce dependence on labeled InSAR samples, a transfer learning strategy was adopted, in which the TCN was pre-trained using simulated displacement sequences and fine-tuned with labeled InSAR observations to classify six kinematic patterns: stable, linear, step, piecewise linear, power-law, and undefined. The corridor is generally stable, with a mean displacement rate of −0.26 mm/year and stable points accounting for 77.96% of observations. Linear and step patterns account for 12.66% and 7.87%, respectively. Strong subsidence zones, where the localized displacement rate reaches −28.43 mm/year, are dominated by linear deformation. Pattern-based interpretation further shows that non-stable deformation is associated with Quaternary unconsolidated sediments, paddy soils, fine-grained soil textures, and urban expansion areas. These results indicate that InSAR-derived kinematic patterns provide an effective interpretive layer for linking railway-corridor displacement, temporal evolution, and environmental context.

title: Relaxing the clear-sky assumption: Cloud-tolerant spatiotemporal fusion via mask-guided feature modulation and temporal-memory collaboration
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The precise characterization of dynamic Earth surface processes relies on time-series remote sensing imagery with both high spatial fidelity and frequent temporal coverage. While spatiotemporal fusion (STF) bridges this resolution trade-off by integrating complementary observations, its practical application remains constrained by the idealized ”clear-sky assumption”. This requirement often favors the selection of temporally distant cloud-free acquisitions over temporally closer but cloud-contaminated observations, potentially reducing the relevance of reference information. To address this limitation, we propose CloudSTF, a robust framework designed to achieve high-fidelity reconstruction by effectively exploiting partially occluded observations. Our approach employs a Mask-guided Multi-scale Swin Transformer (M 2 ST) encoder to capture cloud spatial patterns and suppress noise propagation during feature extraction. This is coupled with a Cross-temporal Memory-guided Fusion (CTMF) module that adaptively integrates temporal trends with textural details retrieved from a spatio-temporal memory bank. To validate this paradigm, we introduce the Global Cloud-shrouded Regions (GCR-STF) benchmark, a geographically distributed dataset comprising 24 representative agricultural and urban sites across six continents. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CloudSTF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additional assessments across varying cloud densities and diverse landscapes further demonstrate the robustness and applicability of CloudSTF under realistic cloud-contaminated conditions. These results suggest that CloudSTF provides a reliable solution for continuous Earth monitoring in realistic, cloud-prone environments. Source code and the GCR-STF benchmark are available at https://github.com/Sichen-Lu/CloudSTF .

title: Adaptive background suppression-based plume identification, emission estimation, and ground validation of coal mine methane in Changzhi, Shanxi, China
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: This study developed a coal mine methane remote-sensing monitoring framework centered on adaptive background suppression using high-spatial-resolution multispectral data from Sentinel-2. The framework integrates methane column enhancement retrieval, automated plume detection, and emission flux estimation. Specifically, bilateral filtering and the multi-band single-pass (MBSP) method were used to retrieve methane column enhancements; a methane plume detection algorithm combining NDVI-based stratification, adaptive segmentation, morphological processing, and wind-field constraints was developed; and coal mine methane emission fluxes were quantified using the integrated mass enhancement (IME) method. Application to a pilot coal enterprise in Changzhi during 2024 demonstrated that the proposed framework effectively reduced weak vegetation-background effects and heterogeneous high-intensity interference while preserving plume topological consistency. Sentinel-2 also provided an observation frequency more than eight times higher than that of EMIT. The mean satellite-derived emission rate for the pilot enterprise was 1023.57 ± 266.84 kg ⋅ h − 1 , with a mean relative deviation of 14.47% from ground-based measurements. The relatively large deviations and daily-scale fluctuations observed during some periods were mainly attributed to uncertainties associated with the spectral resolution of Sentinel-2, surface heterogeneity, algorithm parameter settings, and ERA5 wind-field data. A comparison with the EDGAR inventory revealed broad consistency in regional spatial emission patterns. However, the higher-resolution Sentinel-2 data detected potential coal-related emission signals in several grid cells absent from EDGAR, accounting for 22.2% of the potential emission grids identified in Changzhi. On a regional scale, EDGAR’s annual emission estimate for Changzhi was 32.11% higher than the Sentinel-2 annualized estimate derived in this study.

title: De-biasing Skeleton-Based Action Recognition with Convex Hull Adaptive Shift
IterRF: Iterative and Interpretable Mutual Enhancement for Joint Multi-Modal Image Registration and Fusion
OscVision: Oscillator Networks for Low Power Vision Inference
An Adaptive Dynamic AI-driven ParameTerization (ADAPT) framework for global hourly gross primary productivity estimation
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: High-frequency estimation of gross primary productivity (GPP) is crucial for understanding terrestrial carbon dynamics and ecosystem responses to rapidly changing environmental conditions.
